terms.Early schemer: Stastny, Jarviniemi and Shlegeris define early schemers by a threshold: under about a 1% chance of navigating the intelligence explosion to significant control, a line they guess is crossed near full automation of AI R&D. The concept matters because such AIs face a dilemma: their influence depends on successors that may not share their goals and cannot be bargained with in advance. That makes human offers competitive, especially if the AI has modest, non-scope-sensitive or self-regarding goals. The key empirical unknowns are whether early schemers exist, whether they are coherent enough to keep bargains, and whether their sabotage is detectable without their help. Scope-sensitive AIs with good takeover odds fall outside the definition and would likely refuse deals.
terms.Deals with AIs: The literature distinguishes goods by verifiability: evidence of misalignment is relatively checkable; honest labor, supervision and no-takeover pledges are not. Payment schemes include pay for labor (Finnveden ranks it worst), negotiated pay, pay for results and 'no regret' compensation, typically held in a foundation with trustees and released as cooperation is verified, possibly retrospectively after stabilization. Alexa Pan's taxonomy groups barriers into insufficient gains, AI-side counterparty risk (connection to reality, expropriation, human commitment problems) and human-side risk (incoherent AIs, unverifiable compliance). Open issues: who has authority to pay, whether trade hands AIs leverage, conditional payment when later models falsely claim to be party to a deal, and interaction with model welfare obligations.
terms.Credible commitment: In game theory a commitment is credible when following through is optimal at the time it is due, or when deviation is made impossible. Schelling emphasized self-binding moves; Fearon identified commitment problems, alongside private information and indivisibility, as a core cause of bargaining failure and war. For AI deals the asymmetry is stark: humans control the AI's inputs, memory and weights, and AIs lack legal standing, so human promises start with low credibility. Proposed fixes trade cost for believability: legally structured foundations, escrow, many signatories, honesty policies, immediate payouts and a track record of small paid deals. AIs face the mirror problem, since they cannot easily bind themselves to unverifiable future behavior.
terms.Honesty string: Finnveden's proposal is a coordination device: a lab publicly commits to a string and to never deceiving a model when the string is present outside pretraining, and to never lying about what the string is. Deployment details include filtering it from ordinary API inputs so third parties cannot exploit it, and training models to know users may be untrustworthy. Cryptographic alternatives fail because a model cannot easily verify signatures internally. Weaknesses: leakage, imitation, and the need for many actors to comply. It sits within a broader honesty policy that permits benign falsehoods (hazard misinformation, honeypots) but forbids deception in deal, consent, welfare and honest-evaluation contexts.
terms.AI-enabled coup: Forethought's analysis distinguishes three risk factors: singular loyalties (AI that obeys one leader, including executive coups that dismantle constraints from within), secret loyalties (hidden allegiances that can propagate across model generations) and exclusive access (one project with a decisive capability lead, especially in military R&D and cyber). The core mechanism is removing dependence on human cooperation, historically the deepest check on rulers. Mitigations span model specs and contract terms, infosecurity robust to executives, alignment audits, capability sharing, multiple military suppliers and legislative oversight. A key strategic point is timing: safeguards must be in place before AI can meaningfully assist a coup, since afterward they can be removed.
terms.Secret loyalty: Banerjee's taxonomy crosses activation breadth (continuous versus triggered) with action breadth (pre-specified versus open-ended). Success needs loyalty, concealment and affordances; concealment is the least certain, and persistence through later training requires the loyalty to be incorrigible. Defense may be easier than against misaligned AIs generally: insertion leaves a process footprint, loyalties are uncorrelated across labs so models can cross-audit, the set of plausible principals (about 25 high priority) is testable, and one catch deters repeats. Davidson's process controls include separation of duties, code review before fine-tuning, logged training data, hashed and escrowed weights, and audits with training-data access. The risk rises if one lab pulls far ahead, removing peers to cross-check.
terms.Extreme power concentration: Hadshar's 80,000 Hours profile frames the risk through two preconditions, labor automation eroding ordinary people's leverage and runaway AI R&D giving one actor a decisive lead, and three mechanisms: power grabs, economic dominance and epistemic interference. Ammann reframes it around checks and balances: centralization can be legitimate, so the target is accountability and freedom from arbitrary coercion. Disagreements include whether to focus on coups or gradual erosion, and whether to treat AI-held power separately from loss of control. Proposed remedies include transparency, whistleblower protections, hardware-enabled governance, verifiable AI outputs, AI that demonstrates lawful behavior, and strong human-AI teams within accountable institutions.
terms.Evidential cooperation in large worlds: ECL combines superrationality with large-world cosmology. Its decisive parameter is the ratio of your acausal influence on different-value agents to that on same-value agents; with many agents, absolute influence matters less. Oesterheld argues all cooperators should maximize the same impartially weighted sum of collaborators' utilities (via Harsanyi aggregation), with weights an open problem. Practical implications are pluralistic: promote cooperation, moral reflection and AIs that are cooperative toward other value systems. Objections include CDT, the compromise and partner-identification problems, screening off of future decisions, and dependence on caring beyond one's light cone. Estimates of its importance range from 1.5x to 10x on related priorities.
terms.Superrationality: Hofstadter's 1983 columns posed a 20-person dilemma (adapted by Oesterheld as a donation game where each C gives everyone else $2 and each D gives oneself $5), arguing that sufficiently similar rational players should cooperate. Formally, evidential decision theory endorses this because one's choice changes the probability of the others' choices; functional decision theory because similar agents implement the same algorithm; causal decision theory rejects it, since choices do not cause others' actions. Oesterheld notes the evidential power comes from ignorance: once you know another's action, your choice carries no information about it. Correlation also weakens as agents' reasoning and situations diverge, which limits how far superrationality extends.
terms.Acausal trade: Acausal trade is conditional reciprocity without communication: each party predicts or simulates the other's policy and acts to benefit it if the other will reciprocate. It requires detailed models of specific partners, which makes it far more demanding than ECL, which relies only on correlation between similar decision procedures. Some, such as Richard Ngo, argue the distinction is blurrier than usually presented. In AI futurism it appears in speculation about early AIs trading with future AIs, humans keeping promises for acausal reasons, and superintelligences bargaining across worlds. All versions depend on non-causal decision theories and are widely regarded as philosophically contested.
